Budapest on foot

Wizzy knows 50 places in Budapest, from the big sights to the corners most people walk straight past. Start a walk, put your phone away, and Wizzy taps you on the shoulder when there's something worth looking up at.

The must-sees

  • Buda Castle

    Palace

    The palace was rebuilt again and again after sieges, last after heavy damage in 1945. Today it holds the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the National Széchényi Library.

    Look for: By the gate above the funicular, a bronze turul, the mythical bird of the Magyars, spreads its wings over the river.

  • Dohány Street Synagogue

    Building · 1859

    Ludwig Förster designed it, and it was completed in 1859. In its courtyard lie victims of the 1944–45 ghetto, and behind it Imre Varga’s metal weeping willow carries the names of Holocaust victims.

  • Fisherman’s Bastion

    Viewpoint · 1902

    Frigyes Schulek built it between 1895 and 1902 as a decorative lookout, not a fortification. The name recalls the fishermen’s guild that is said to have defended this stretch of the medieval walls.

    Look for: Between the bastion and the church, a bronze St Stephen sits on horseback, holding the apostolic double cross.

  • Great Market Hall

    Market · 1897

    Samu Pecz designed it, and it opened in 1897. Paprika, salami and produce are sold on the ground floor, and food stalls fill the gallery above.

    Look for: Head down to the basement for the fish counters and stalls of pickled vegetables.

  • Heroes’ Square

    Square

    The Millennium Monument was begun for the 1896 celebration of a thousand years since the Magyar arrival. Archangel Gabriel stands on the column, and the seven Magyar chieftains ride below.

    Look for: In front of the column, a stone slab remembers the heroes who gave their lives for Hungary’s freedom.

  • Hungarian Parliament Building

    Civic building · 1904

    Imre Steindl designed it after a competition in the 1880s, and it was completed in 1904; he went blind and died before it was finished. The Holy Crown of Hungary is kept under the dome.

  • Hungarian State Opera

    Culture · 1884

    Miklós Ybl designed it, and it opened in 1884. Gustav Mahler was its director for a few seasons around 1890.

    Look for: Sphinxes guard the carriage ramps at either side of the entrance.

  • Matthias Church

    Church

    It takes its name from King Matthias Corvinus, who married here twice. Franz Joseph and Elisabeth were crowned in it in 1867, and Frigyes Schulek restored it in neo-Gothic style in the late 19th century.

    Look for: Inside, nearly every wall and pillar is painted with patterns and figures, a 19th-century tribute to medieval Hungary.

  • Shoes on the Danube Bank

    Landmark · 2005

    Can Togay and Gyula Pauer created the memorial in 2005. It remembers the Jews shot into the river by Arrow Cross militiamen in the winter of 1944–45, who were made to take off their shoes first.

    Look for: The shoes are modelled on styles of the 1940s: men’s boots, women’s heels and small children’s shoes.

  • St. Stephen’s Basilica

    Church · 1905

    It took more than fifty years to build; the first dome collapsed in 1868 and had to be rebuilt. It keeps the mummified right hand of St Stephen, Hungary’s first king.

    Look for: Above the main door, the Latin words say: I am the way, the truth and the life.

  • Széchenyi Baths

    Venue · 1913

    It opened in 1913, fed by thermal water from a deep well. Chess players standing in the hot water play here all year round.

    Look for: Outside, the middle pool is the cooler one for swimming, and the two on either side are warm for soaking.

  • Széchenyi Chain Bridge

    Bridge · 1849

    Count István Széchenyi pushed for it, the English engineer William Tierney Clark designed it, and the Scot Adam Clark built it; it opened in 1849. German troops blew it up in January 1945, and it was rebuilt by 1949.

    Look for: Check the lions’ mouths. Legend says the sculptor was mocked because they had no tongues; they do, but you can’t see them from below.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Budapest and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Budapest passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
